html:
The Great Māhele of 1848 divided the land of the Kingdom of Hawaii between the king, the government and the chiefs. Until then, all land had been held by the king and worked by commoners under chiefs.

King Kamehameha III agreed to it under pressure from foreign advisers who wanted secure title. Laws in 1850 let commoners claim the plots they farmed and let foreigners buy land.

Few commoners managed to file claims. Much land soon passed to foreigners, above all sugar planters. The loss of land weakened Native Hawaiians and set the stage for the overthrow of 1893.
